chapter.name: Cell: The Building Block of Life

questions.q: When two points are viewed from the near point of the eye (about 25 cm), the smallest distance at which the unaided human eye can still see them as two separate points is about
questions.a: About 0.1 mm. This is the limit of resolution of the human eye.

questions.q: In 1665 Robert Hooke saw small box-like compartments through his self-designed microscope and named them 'cells'. What was he examining?
questions.a: A thin slice of cork.

questions.q: Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II. Column I: 1. Resolution; 2. Contrast; 3. Magnification; 4. Electron microscope. Column II: (a) the difference in brightness between various parts of an object; (b) making an object appear larger; (c) a measure of clarity; (d) uses a beam of electrons instead of light to form the image.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d: resolution is the measure of clarity, contrast is the difference in brightness between parts, magnification makes the object look larger, and an electron microscope uses a beam of electrons.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Most cells cannot be seen with the unaided eye. Reason (R): Most cells are smaller than 0.1 mm, the limit of resolution of the human eye.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: a cell is usually smaller than the limit of resolution of the eye, so a lens system is needed to see it.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name the two lenses whose combination magnifies an object in a school light microscope. (b) How is the total magnification of the microscope found from them?
questions.a: (a) The objective lens and the eyepiece. (b) Total magnification = magnifying power of the eyepiece x magnifying power of the objective lens (for example 10X x 10X = 100X).
s: (a) Objective lens and eyepiece named
(b) Total magnification = eyepiece power x objective power

questions.q: Salma's microscope has a 10X eyepiece. (a) Which objective lens must she use to get a total magnification of 400X? (b) A cell is 15 µm across. How large, in mm, will it appear at 400X? (1 mm = 1000 µm)
questions.a: (a) 400 / 10 = 40, so the 40X objective. (b) 15 µm x 400 = 6000 µm = 6 mm.
s: (a) 40X objective, since 10 x 40 = 400

questions.q: Three objects are to be studied: a chicken egg, a bacterium about 2 µm across, and a ribosome, which is far smaller than a micrometre and is studied at the nanometre scale. For each, say whether the unaided eye, a light microscope or an electron microscope is needed, and give the reason in each case.
questions.a: Chicken egg: unaided eye, because it is centimetres across, far above the 0.1 mm limit of resolution. Bacterium (2 µm = 0.002 mm): smaller than 0.1 mm, so the eye cannot resolve it, but a light microscope magnifies it enough to be seen. Ribosome: an electron microscope, because only a beam of electrons shows detail at the nanometre scale, beyond what a light microscope reveals.
s: Chicken egg: unaided eye; well above the 0.1 mm limit
Bacterium: light microscope; 0.002 mm is below the eye's limit but within a light microscope's reach
Ribosome: electron microscope; nanometre-scale detail needs a beam of electrons

questions.q: A school laboratory has eyepieces of 10X and 15X and objective lenses of 10X and 40X, and any eyepiece can be used with any objective. Arif wants to view a bacterium 5 µm across so that its image appears at least 1 mm across. (a) List the total magnification of all four combinations. (b) Work out how large, in mm, the 5 µm bacterium appears with each combination. (c) Which combinations meet Arif's need, and which of them has the lowest total magnification? (d) Arif then wants to see the ribosomes inside the bacterium. Explain why none of these combinations will do, and what instrument he needs.
questions.a: (a) 10X x 10X = 100X; 10X x 40X = 400X; 15X x 10X = 150X; 15X x 40X = 600X. (b) 5 µm x 100 = 0.5 mm; x 400 = 2 mm; x 150 = 0.75 mm; x 600 = 3 mm. (c) Only 400X (2 mm) and 600X (3 mm) reach 1 mm; the lowest of these is 400X (10X eyepiece with 40X objective). (d) A light microscope uses visible light and cannot show structures at the nanometre scale; an electron microscope, which uses a beam of electrons, is needed to see such fine detail.
s: (a) Four totals: 100X, 400X, 150X, 600X
(b) Image sizes 0.5 mm, 2 mm, 0.75 mm, 3 mm
(c) 400X and 600X meet the need; 400X is the lowest
(d) Light microscope cannot resolve nanometre-scale detail; electron microscope (beam of electrons) needed

questions.q: The cell membrane is made up mainly of
questions.a: Lipids (fats) and proteins.

questions.q: In the fluid-mosaic model, why is the cell membrane described as 'fluid'?
questions.a: Because the molecules in it can move sideways, flip and rotate within the membrane.
o: Its molecules can move sideways, flip and rotate within it
It is made of water held between two layers
It lets every liquid pass through it freely
It is filled with a watery fluid called cell sap

questions.q: True or False: 'Proteins embedded in the cell membrane act like gatekeepers that help substances pass through it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. In the fluid-mosaic model the lipid bilayer has proteins embedded in it, and these proteins act like gatekeepers in helping substances pass through the membrane.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: proteins embedded in the lipid bilayer help substances pass, like gatekeepers

questions.q: (a) What does it mean to say the cell membrane is selectively permeable? (b) In Activity 2.2, with a potato piece in salt solution, name one substance the membrane lets through and one it does not.
questions.a: (a) It allows some substances to pass through it while blocking others. (b) Water passes through; the salt (or sugar) molecules do not.
s: (a) Lets some substances pass and blocks others
(b) Water passes; salt or sugar does not

questions.q: Read the statements. I. In an isotonic solution, the solute concentration outside the cell equals that inside it. II. A cell kept in a hypotonic solution loses water. III. In osmosis, water moves from a dilute solution towards a concentrated solution across a selectively permeable membrane. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: a hypotonic solution has less solute outside than inside, so water enters the cell and it gains water.

questions.q: The solute concentration inside some cheek cells is 5 units. One cell is placed in each of three solutions: P with 2 units, Q with 5 units and R with 9 units of solute. For each solution, name the type of solution (isotonic, hypotonic or hypertonic) and predict what happens to the cell.
questions.a: P (2 < 5): hypotonic; water enters the cell by osmosis and it swells. Q (5 = 5): isotonic; no net movement of water, so the cell stays the same. R (9 > 5): hypertonic; water leaves the cell and it shrinks.
s: P: hypotonic; water moves in, cell swells
Q: isotonic; no net change
R: hypertonic; water moves out, cell shrinks

questions.q: A science club in Mysuru compares a plant cell and an animal cell, as in Activity 2.3. They keep Rhoeo leaf peels and cheek-cell smears in plain water and in 20 per cent sugar solution for half an hour. For each leaf peel they count, out of 50 cells, how many show the inner content pulled away from the cell wall. For the cheek cells they measure the average width, which was 60 µm at the start. Plain water: leaf 0 of 50, cheek 61 µm. 20 per cent sugar: leaf 45 of 50, cheek 45 µm. (a) For the 20 per cent sugar solution, find the percentage of leaf cells whose content pulled away and the percentage decrease in cheek-cell width. (b) In the 20 per cent sugar solution, in which direction did water move, and is the solution hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic to these cells? (c) The outer boundary of the leaf cells stayed the same size in both liquids. Which structure explains this? (d) A club member concludes, 'The sugar solution did not affect the leaf cells, because their size did not change.' Evaluate this conclusion using the data.
questions.a: (a) 45/50 x 100 = 90 per cent of leaf cells; (60 - 45)/60 x 100 = 25 per cent decrease in cheek-cell width. (b) Water moved out of the cells into the sugar solution by osmosis, so the solution is hypertonic to the cells (more solute outside than inside). (c) The rigid cell wall of the leaf cells keeps their outer shape, while cheek cells have no cell wall and shrink. (d) The conclusion is wrong: 90 per cent of the leaf cells lost water, since their inner content shrank and pulled away from the wall; the rigid wall only hid the loss in outer size.
s: (a) 90 per cent of leaf cells; 25 per cent decrease in cheek-cell width
(b) Water moved out of the cells by osmosis; the solution is hypertonic
(c) The rigid cell wall keeps the leaf cell's outer shape; cheek cells lack it
(d) Wrong: 90 per cent of leaf cells lost water (content pulled away); the wall hid the change in size

questions.q: The words 'prokaryotic' and 'eukaryotic' both contain the Greek word 'karyon'. What does 'karyon' mean?
questions.a: Nucleus ('pro' means primitive and 'eu' means true).

questions.q: In Activity 2.3, which stain is added to the slide of human cheek cells?
questions.a: Methylene blue. The onion or Rhoeo peel is mounted in safranin.

questions.q: Pooja sees tiny crystals of calcium oxalate lying in the cytoplasm of some cells, with no membrane around them. She concludes, 'These must be bacterial cells, because the stored crystals have no membrane around them.' Which is the best response?
questions.a: She is wrong: such crystals are cell inclusions stored in the cytoplasm of some plant cells, which are eukaryotic, so a stored material without a membrane does not show that a cell is prokaryotic.
o: Wrong: such crystals are cell inclusions found in some plant cells, which are eukaryotic
Right: anything in a cell that has no membrane around it shows the cell is prokaryotic
Right: crystals of calcium oxalate are stored only in bacterial cells
Wrong: the crystals are membrane-bound organelles, so the cells are eukaryotic

questions.q: Match each structure in Column I with its description in Column II. Column I: 1. Cytoskeleton; 2. Nucleoid; 3. Cytoplasm; 4. Cell wall. Column II: (a) a semi-fluid, jelly-like substance inside the cell; (b) a rigid but permeable covering, made mainly of cellulose in plants; (c) a network of fine fibres that supports and shapes a eukaryotic cell; (d) the region that holds the genetic material of a bacterial cell.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: the cytoskeleton is the network of fine fibres, the nucleoid holds a bacterium's genetic material, the cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance and the cell wall is the rigid, permeable covering.

questions.q: Assertion (A): When a Rhoeo leaf peel is kept in concentrated sugar solution, its cells lose water but their outer boundaries stay the same. Reason (R): The cell wall is permeable, so water and some dissolved minerals can pass through it.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The boundaries stay the same because the cell wall is rigid and keeps its shape; its permeability is a separate fact.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A report on cell Z says: about 8 µm across; has a cell wall; has ribosomes; its DNA is a single circular molecule with proteins; no membrane-bound organelles were seen. Ravi says Z is eukaryotic because it has a cell wall and ribosomes, like a plant cell. (a) Decide whether Z is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and name the evidence that decides it. (b) Explain why the cell wall and ribosomes do not settle the question.
questions.a: (a) Prokaryotic: its DNA is a single circular molecule (a nucleoid, not a membrane-bound nucleus) and it has no membrane-bound organelles; its size of 8 µm also fits the 1 to 10 µm range. (b) Both kinds of cell can have them: bacteria and fungi as well as plants have a cell wall, and the bacterial cell in Fig. 2.10 also has ribosomes, so these features are shared and cannot tell the two types apart.
s: (a) Prokaryotic: single circular DNA (nucleoid) and no membrane-bound organelles
(b) Cell wall and ribosomes are found in bacterial cells too, so they do not separate the types

questions.q: Arjun says, 'Eukaryotic cells are 10 to 100 µm across, so an organism made of just one cell must be prokaryotic.' Is he right? Explain using the comparison of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and state the feature that actually decides the type of a cell.
questions.a: No. Prokaryotic cells are usually unicellular, but eukaryotic cells can be unicellular or multicellular, so being one cell does not make an organism prokaryotic. The type is decided by the cell's organisation: a eukaryotic cell has a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, while a prokaryotic cell has a nucleoid and no membrane-bound organelles.
s: Verdict: No, Arjun is wrong
Eukaryotic cells can be unicellular or multicellular, so one cell does not mean prokaryotic
The deciding feature is a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles (eukaryotic) versus a nucleoid with none (prokaryotic)

questions.q: Slide X holds bacterial cells and Slide Y holds onion peel cells. Apply what you know about these two kinds of cell to state, for each slide: (a) whether a cell wall is present; (b) whether the genetic material is enclosed by a membrane, and the name of the region that holds it if it is not; (c) whether membrane-bound organelles are present; (d) the diameter of a typical cell of that kind (prokaryotic or eukaryotic), as given in the chapter's comparison table; (e) whether the cell is prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
questions.a: (a) X: yes; Y: yes. (b) X: no, it lies in a region called the nucleoid; Y: yes, in a membrane-bound nucleus. (c) X: absent; Y: present. (d) X: a typical prokaryotic cell is 1 to 10 µm; Y: a typical eukaryotic cell is 10 to 100 µm. (e) X: prokaryotic; Y: eukaryotic.
s: (a) Cell wall present in both X and Y
(b) X: genetic material not enclosed, in the nucleoid; Y: in a membrane-bound nucleus
(c) Membrane-bound organelles absent in X, present in Y
(d) Typical prokaryotic cell 1 to 10 µm (X); typical eukaryotic cell 10 to 100 µm (Y)
(e) X prokaryotic; Y eukaryotic

questions.q: The functional segments of DNA are called
questions.a: Genes.

questions.q: (a) Arrange these from the largest to the smallest: DNA molecule, nucleus, gene, chromosome. (b) Give the reason why a gene comes after DNA in your order.
questions.a: (a) Nucleus, chromosome, DNA molecule, gene. (b) A gene is a functional segment of a DNA molecule, so it is a part of the DNA.
s: (a) Nucleus > chromosome > DNA > gene
(b) A gene is a functional segment of DNA

questions.q: Answer briefly about the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell. (a) What kind of covering does the nucleus have? (b) What do the pores in this covering allow? (c) What is the dense round body inside the nucleus called, and what is made there?
questions.a: (a) A double-layered nuclear membrane. (b) Transfer of material between the nucleus and the cytoplasm. (c) The nucleolus; ribosomal subunits are made there.
s: (a) Double-layered nuclear membrane
(b) Pores allow transfer of material between nucleus and cytoplasm
(c) Nucleolus, where ribosomal subunits are made

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Chromosomes are composed of DNA and specific proteins. II. In prokaryotic cells, the DNA is a single circular molecule associated with specific proteins. III. The nuclear membrane is a single layer with no pores. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: the nuclear membrane is double-layered and has pores.

questions.q: True or False: 'Complete ribosomes are assembled inside the nucleolus and then leave the nucleus.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The nucleolus makes only the ribosomal subunits; these leave the nucleus, and one large and one small subunit assemble into a ribosome in the cytoplasm.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: subunits made in the nucleolus assemble into a ribosome in the cytoplasm

questions.q: A teacher wants her class to see rod-shaped chromosomes. In a trial she counts 200 cells on each of three slides. Slide 1, onion root tip: 46 cells show rod-shaped structures in the nucleus, the rest show a tangled mass of threads. Slide 2, human cheek cells: every nucleus shows only a tangled mass of threads. Slide 3, a smear of mature human red blood cells: no nucleus is seen in any cell. (a) What are the rod-shaped structures, and what percentage of the cells on Slide 1 show them? (b) Why do they appear on Slide 1 and not on Slide 2? (c) Explain what is seen on Slide 3. (d) Which slide should she use for the lesson? Justify your choice from the data.
questions.a: (a) They are chromosomes; 46/200 x 100 = 23 per cent of the cells show them. (b) Chromosomes become visible only when a cell is about to divide; the cells of a growing root tip divide continuously, while cheek cells here are not dividing, so their DNA is seen only as chromatin, a tangled mass of thread-like material. (c) Mature red blood cells have no nucleus (they are enucleate), so neither chromatin nor chromosomes can be seen. (d) Slide 1: it is the only slide with any cells showing chromosomes (about 23 per cent), and the other cells on it show chromatin for comparison.
s: (a) Chromosomes; 23 per cent of Slide 1 cells
(b) Visible only in cells about to divide; root-tip cells divide, cheek cells show only chromatin
(c) Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, so nothing is seen
(d) Slide 1: the only slide with chromosomes (23 per cent of cells)

questions.q: Under an electron microscope, Cell M shows a dense round body inside a double membrane with pores. In Cell N the DNA is a single circular molecule with proteins, lying in the cytoplasm with no membrane around it. Which conclusion is correct?
questions.a: Cell M can make ribosomal subunits in its nucleolus (the dense round body in a nucleus), while Cell N's DNA lies in a nucleoid, so N is a prokaryotic cell.
o: M makes ribosomal subunits in its nucleolus; N has a nucleoid and is prokaryotic
M is prokaryotic, because its DNA is enclosed by a double membrane
N carries no genes, because it has no nucleus
The dense round body in M is a chromosome, so M is about to divide

questions.q: Ribosomes, found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, are the sites of
questions.a: Protein synthesis.

questions.q: The endoplasmic reticulum spreads like a network in the cytoplasm. With which structure is it continuous?
questions.a: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope.
o: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope
The inner membrane of the mitochondrion
The membrane of the central vacuole

questions.q: A sperm cell has its lysosomal enzymes, but because of a defect it cannot release them when it meets an egg. What is the most likely result?
questions.a: The outer layer of the egg is not broken down, so fertilisation cannot take place: the sperm's lysosomal enzymes are what break down that layer.
o: The egg's outer layer is not broken down, so fertilisation cannot take place
The sperm runs out of energy, because lysosomes supply the energy for its movement
Waste piles up inside the sperm, but fertilisation goes on normally
The egg's outer layer is broken down by the egg's own ribosomes instead

questions.q: The chapter gives each organelle a nickname. Match Column I with Column II. Column I: 1. Protein factories; 2. Manufacturing factory; 3. Packaging and shipping centre; 4. Clean-up system. Column II: (a) Golgi apparatus; (b) lysosomes; (c) ribosomes; (d) endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: ribosomes are the protein factories, the ER the manufacturing factory, the Golgi apparatus the packaging and shipping centre, and lysosomes the clean-up system.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Lysosomes keep the cell clean and healthy. Reason (R): Lysosomes are sacs of enzymes that can break down unwanted proteins, carbohydrates, fats and damaged parts of the cell.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the enzymes in lysosomes break down waste and damaged parts, so these do not pile up in the cell.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In a gland cell, the ribosomes and the ER work normally, but the Golgi apparatus stops working. State two effects this would have on the cell.
questions.a: (1) Proteins and lipids made by the ribosomes and ER would not be modified, sorted and packaged into vesicles, so they could not be transported or secreted. (2) New lysosomes, which the Golgi apparatus helps form, would not be made, so the cell's clean-up would suffer.
s: Proteins/lipids not modified, sorted and packed into vesicles, so not transported or secreted
Lysosome formation stops, so waste clearing suffers

questions.q: A gland cell secretes two products: a fat-based hormone and a protein enzyme. (a) Trace each product from the organelle where it is made to its release from the cell. (b) A chemical strips the ribosomes off the rough ER but leaves the smooth ER and the Golgi apparatus unharmed. Predict which product's making falls and which carries on, and justify both.
questions.a: (a) Enzyme: made by ribosomes on the rough ER, then the Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages it into vesicles that carry it to the plasma membrane for secretion. Hormone: made on the smooth ER, then packaged by the Golgi apparatus into vesicles for secretion. (b) The enzyme's making falls, because ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis and the rough ER needs them for protein synthesis and secretion. The hormone carries on, because the smooth ER has no ribosomes and makes fats and hormones without them, and the Golgi apparatus still packages it.
s: (a) Enzyme: rough ER ribosomes -> Golgi -> vesicles -> secreted; hormone: smooth ER -> Golgi -> vesicles -> secreted
(b) Enzyme falls: ribosomes, the sites of protein synthesis, are lost from the rough ER
(b) Hormone carries on: smooth ER has no ribosomes and still makes it; Golgi still packages it

questions.q: Two animal cells, X and Y, are of similar size, but X has many more mitochondria than Y. Which conclusion is the most reasonable?
questions.a: Cell X can break down more glucose in cellular respiration and release more energy, stored as ATP, for its activities.
o: X can release more energy, stored as ATP, for its activities
X can make more of its own food by photosynthesis
X can store more starch in its cytoplasm
X keeps itself firmer with a larger central vacuole

questions.q: Plastids that have no pigment and store food such as starch, oils or proteins are called
questions.a: Leucoplasts.

questions.q: The semi-fluid substance inside a chloroplast, in which the sugars made in photosynthesis are stored along with starch granules, is called the
questions.a: Stroma.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Chromoplasts in flower petals help in pollination. Reason (R): Chromoplasts are colourless plastids that store starch, oils or proteins.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The yellow, orange or red pigments of chromoplasts colour the petals and attract pollinators; the colourless plastids that store food are leucoplasts.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False: 'Like mitochondria, chloroplasts are surrounded by two membranes.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A mitochondrion has a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane, and chloroplasts are also double-membrane-bound organelles.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: both have an outer and an inner membrane (double-membrane-bound)

questions.q: (a) What do the Greek words 'chroma' and 'leukos' mean? (b) Use these meanings to explain the names chromoplast and leucoplast.
questions.a: (a) Chroma means colour; leukos means white. (b) Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments (yellow, orange or red), while leucoplasts lack pigment and are colourless (white).
s: (a) Chroma = colour; leukos = white
(b) Chromoplasts carry coloured pigments; leucoplasts have no pigment

questions.q: Riya compares a typical plant cell with a typical animal cell. (a) to (c): for each structure, state whether it is found in the plant cell, the animal cell or both, and give its one main job: (a) mitochondria; (b) chloroplasts; (c) a large central vacuole. (d) Vacuoles are sometimes present in animal cells. State how they differ from the central vacuole of a plant cell and what they do.
questions.a: (a) Both; they break down glucose in cellular respiration and release energy stored as ATP. (b) Plant cell; their chlorophyll absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis. (c) Plant cell (mature); it stores water, minerals, sugars and waste and keeps the cell firm. (d) They are much smaller than the large central vacuole of a plant cell, and they store materials only for a short time (temporary storage).
s: (a) Mitochondria: both; release energy as ATP by cellular respiration
(b) Chloroplasts: plant; photosynthesis using chlorophyll
(c) Large central vacuole: plant; stores water, minerals, sugars, waste and keeps the cell firm
(d) Animal-cell vacuoles are small, not large like the plant's; they store materials temporarily

questions.q: Kunal is making a labelled model of a plant cell for a science fair. He must show which organelle does each of these jobs and the part of it that does the work: (a) releasing energy from glucose for the cell's activities; (b) absorbing light energy to make sugars; (c) giving a ripe fruit its orange colour; (d) storing water and keeping the cell firm. (e) His friend says the model should leave out mitochondria, because in a plant the chloroplasts already supply the energy. Decide whether the friend is right, with a reason.
questions.a: (a) Mitochondrion: glucose is broken down in cellular respiration, and the folded inner membrane (cristae) gives more surface area for the reactions; the energy is stored as ATP. (b) Chloroplast: chlorophyll in the disc-shaped membrane structures within the stroma absorbs light. (c) Chromoplast: its yellow, orange or red pigments. (d) Central vacuole: its cell sap holds water, which keeps up pressure in the cell. (e) The friend is wrong. Chloroplasts make food (sugars) using light, but the energy in that food is released for the cell's activities in the mitochondria as ATP, so a plant cell needs both.
s: (a) Mitochondrion; cristae, energy stored as ATP
(b) Chloroplast; chlorophyll in disc-shaped structures in the stroma
(c) Chromoplast; its coloured pigments
(d) Central vacuole; cell sap holds water and keeps the cell firm
(e) Friend wrong: chloroplasts make food, mitochondria release its energy as ATP; both needed

questions.q: In flowering plants, meiosis takes place in the
questions.a: Anthers (to form pollen grains) and the ovaries (to form egg cells).

questions.q: In Activity 2.5, a drop of dilute hydrochloric acid is put on the onion root tips before staining. Why?
questions.a: To soften the tissue.
o: To make the roots grow faster

questions.q: Meena grows, preserves, softens and stains her onion roots exactly as in Activity 2.5, but before squashing she uses a piece from higher up the root instead of the tip portion. On her slide all the cells look alike and none show the different structures seen during cell division. Which is the most likely reason?
questions.a: Only the cells of the growing tip of the root divide continuously and show the different stages of cell division; her piece came from a part of the root whose cells were not dividing.
o: Only cells at the growing root tip divide continuously; her piece had no dividing cells
Aceto-carmine stains only the cells that are not dividing
Root cells divide only by meiosis, which cannot be seen under a microscope
Dilute HCl joins the cells together, so the stages cannot be told apart

questions.q: In humans, meiosis occurs only in the cells of certain organs. (a) Name the organ in males and the gamete it produces. (b) Name the organ in females and the gamete it produces.
questions.a: (a) Testes; sperm. (b) Ovaries; eggs.
s: (a) Testes, producing sperm
(b) Ovaries, producing eggs

questions.q: True or False: 'In meiosis, the second division halves the chromosome number of the cells a second time.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chromosome number is halved in the first division; the second division is similar to mitosis, so each of the four daughter cells keeps half the parent's chromosome number.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: halving happens in the first division; the second is like mitosis and keeps the half number

questions.q: The body cells of a plant have 24 chromosomes. A cell in its anther divides by meiosis. (a) After the first division, how many cells are there and how many chromosomes does each have? (b) After the second division, how many cells are there and how many chromosomes does each have? (c) If a sperm cell from this plant fuses with an egg cell of the same plant species at fertilisation, how many chromosomes does the fertilised egg have?
questions.a: (a) 2 cells, each with 12 chromosomes (halved in the first division). (b) 4 cells, each with 12 chromosomes (the second division is like mitosis). (c) 12 + 12 = 24, the original number is restored.
s: (a) 2 cells with 12 chromosomes each
(b) 4 cells with 12 chromosomes each
(c) 12 + 12 = 24 in the fertilised egg

questions.q: A vaccine unit in Hyderabad grows animal cells in culture flasks. Last month it ran 40 flasks in Room A, which is kept sterile, and 40 flasks in Room B, which is not; both rooms were kept at the same temperature and moisture. In Room A, 2 flasks were spoiled by germs; in Room B, 14 flasks were spoiled. Keeping Room B sterile as well would cost Rs 30,000 more each month, and every spoiled flask wastes material worth Rs 5,000. (a) Find the percentage of flasks spoiled in each room. (b) Besides sterile conditions, name two other conditions that must be kept right for a cell culture. (c) Why must the medium in each flask be nutrient-rich? (d) Should the unit pay to keep Room B sterile? Decide, using the costs.
questions.a: (a) Room A: 2/40 x 100 = 5 per cent; Room B: 14/40 x 100 = 35 per cent. (b) Any two of: the right temperature, the right acidic or alkaline conditions, the right moisture. (c) The cells are outside the body and must take everything they need to grow and multiply from the medium. (d) Yes. If Room B spoiled flasks at Room A's rate, it would lose about 2 flasks instead of 14, saving 12 x Rs 5,000 = Rs 60,000 a month, which is more than the Rs 30,000 extra cost, a net saving of about Rs 30,000.
s: (a) A: 5 per cent; B: 35 per cent
(b) Two of: right temperature, acidic or alkaline conditions, moisture
(c) Cells outside the body get what they need to grow and multiply from the medium
(d) Yes: 12 fewer spoiled flasks save Rs 60,000, more than the Rs 30,000 cost

questions.q: The body cells of an animal species have 20 chromosomes, and each individual begins life as a single fertilised egg. (a) Name the type of cell division that increases the number of cells as the embryo grows, and say why it keeps the genetic information the same in body cells. (b) If every cell divides once in each round, how many cells are there after 10 rounds, starting from the fertilised egg? (c) How many chromosomes does each of these body cells have? (d) In the reproductive organs, one cell divides by meiosis. How many gametes form, and how many chromosomes does each carry? (e) Explain why the offspring of this species resemble their parents but are not exactly the same.
questions.a: (a) Mitosis; each daughter cell gets the same DNA and the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell. (b) The number doubles each round: 2 to the power 10 = 1024 cells. (c) 20, the same as the fertilised egg. (d) 4 gametes, each with 10 chromosomes. (e) Gametes made by meiosis create variation; at fertilisation two gametes from two individuals combine, so the offspring gets genetic material from both parents and resembles them without being identical.
s: (a) Mitosis; daughter cells get the same DNA and chromosome number
(c) 20 chromosomes in each body cell
(d) 4 gametes with 10 chromosomes each
(e) Meiosis creates variation; gametes from two parents combine, so offspring resemble but differ

questions.q: Match each scientist in Column I with the year and idea in Column II. Column I: 1. Matthias Schleiden; 2. Theodor Schwann; 3. Rudolf Virchow; 4. Gottlieb Haberlandt. Column II: (a) 1855, new cells are formed only from pre-existing cells; (b) 1902, a mature plant cell can develop into a complete plant; (c) 1838, all plants are made up of cells; (d) 1839, all animals are made up of cells.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b: Schleiden (1838) for plants, Schwann (1839) for animals, Virchow (1855) for cells from pre-existing cells, and Haberlandt (1902) for totipotency.

questions.q: A tumour whose cells can invade nearby tissues and even spread to other parts of the body to form new tumours is
questions.a: A malignant (cancerous) tumour.
o: a sign of Programmed Cell Death

questions.q: Nisha keeps a few yeast cells in sugar water. Next day there are many more yeast cells, although she added nothing but sugar water. Which statement of the classical Cell Theory does this observation directly support?
questions.a: All cells arise from pre-existing cells: the new yeast cells could only have come from the yeast cells already present, by cell division, not from the sugar water.
o: All cells arise from pre-existing cells
All living organisms are made up of one or more cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure and function
New cells can form from the sugar in the water

questions.q: True or False: 'Plant cells show contact inhibition because they have rigid cell walls.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Because of their rigid cell walls, plant cells do NOT show contact inhibition; they follow a different pattern of growth. Contact inhibition is seen in many animal cells.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: rigid walls mean plant cells do not show contact inhibition; many animal cells do

questions.q: Give the meaning of each term in one line. (a) Contact inhibition. (b) Programmed Cell Death. (c) Totipotency.
questions.a: (a) In many animal cells, cell division stops when the cells come in contact with neighbouring cells. (b) A genetically regulated and organised process of selective cell destruction. (c) The ability of a living plant cell, even a mature one, to develop into a complete plant when given suitable nutrients and conditions.
s: (a) Division stops when animal cells touch neighbouring cells
(b) Genetically regulated, organised selective destruction of cells
(c) A plant cell, even mature, can develop into a whole plant

questions.q: Assertion (A): Programmed Cell Death is harmful to a developing human embryo. Reason (R): Programmed Cell Death removes the cells between the developing digits.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. By removing the cells between the digits, Programmed Cell Death forms separate fingers; it is essential for normal development, not harmful.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: Read the statements. I. Programmed Cell Death is a random, uncontrolled destruction of cells. II. A malignant tumour can invade nearby tissues and spread to other parts of the body. III. Every cell has a definite life span, and dead cells are replaced by new cells that carry out the same function. Which of these are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: Programmed Cell Death is a genetically regulated and organised process of selective cell destruction, not a random one.

questions.q: A biology teacher in Bhopal uses a simple model. She tells the class that about 1 per cent of the cells in our body are replaced every day, and asks them to imagine a patch of skin with 50,000 cells in which, in the same way, about 1 per cent of the cells are replaced each day while the total stays the same. (a) How many cells of the patch are replaced each day? (b) How many are replaced in 10 days? (c) Why do old cells in the body need to be replaced at all? (d) Name the type of cell division that makes the new skin cells, and say why it is the right type.
questions.a: (a) 1 per cent of 50,000 = 500 cells a day. (b) 500 x 10 = 5,000 cells in 10 days. (c) Every cell has a definite life span; cells die when they are no longer needed (or are damaged), and dead cells are replaced by new cells that do the same job. (d) Mitosis, because it gives genetically identical daughter cells with the same DNA and chromosome number, so the new cells can do the same job.
s: (a) 500 cells a day
(b) 5,000 cells in 10 days
(c) Every cell has a definite life span; dead cells are replaced by new ones doing the same job
(d) Mitosis: identical daughter cells with the same DNA

questions.q: In a pond water sample, students find a living organism made of just one cell, about 3 µm across, with its DNA lying in a nucleoid and no membrane-bound organelles. In a flask of nutrients, its numbers grow as each cell divides. Ravi claims, 'This organism does not fit the Cell Theory, because it is not made of many cells and has no nucleus.' Test Ravi's claim against each statement of the classical Cell Theory and give your verdict.
questions.a: Statement 1 says living organisms are made of one OR more cells, so a one-celled organism fits. Statement 2: its single cell carries out all its life processes, so the cell is its basic unit of structure and function. Statement 3: its new cells come from the division of existing cells, so they arise from pre-existing cells. Having no nucleus only makes it a prokaryotic cell; it does not place it outside the theory. Verdict: Ravi is wrong; the organism fits the Cell Theory.
s: Statement 1: one or more cells, so a unicellular organism fits
Statement 2: its single cell is the basic unit of structure and function
Statement 3: new cells come from division of existing cells
No nucleus only makes it prokaryotic; verdict: Ravi is wrong
